overview: These map fragments belong to Arakan’s Mrauk U kingdom, founded in 1430 and conquered in 1784 to 1785. Their gaps do not mean the kingdom vanished between snapshots. The 1492 to 1530 outline is badly displaced and omits Mrauk U itself; later outlines are approximate. The imported “Indian princely state” label for 1700 to 1783 is misleading: this was still an independent kingdom, before British rule.

sections.title: A coastal kingdom with far-reaching connections

items.text: Arakan’s mountain barrier separated it from the Irrawaddy valley, while rivers and the Bay of Bengal opened routes abroad. Its rulers expanded south toward Sandoway and northwest toward Ramu. Under Min Phalaung, Chittagong came securely under Arakanese control around 1578 and remained so until 1666. Portuguese soldiers, sailors and merchants became important, sometimes troublesome partners.

A silver tanka of King Dharmaraja Hussain, dated to his reign from 1612 to 1622, measures about three centimeters across. Its inscriptions use Arakanese, Bengali and Persian Arabic writing. The ruler combined a Buddhist royal title with a Muslim name. A small coin could announce kingship to people connected with several languages and traditions.

A royal order issued in 1643 allowed Dutch merchants to buy beeswax, lacquer material, indigo and coarse white cloth. Rice purchases depended on supply: more could be sold when it was plentiful, less when scarce. The agreement links farming and craft work to overseas trade, while showing the king trying to control what left his country.

Commerce also included the forced movement of people. Raiders brought captives from Bengal, and Dutch traders sought enslaved workers for distant plantations. The same royal order reserved skilled captives for Arakan instead of allowing their export. This was a policy about retaining labor, not ending slavery. Behind the trade stood people uprooted from their homes and families.

Mrauk U’s waterways carried produce and handmade goods toward its central market. Natural rivers were joined by canals serving both transport and irrigation. Shopping supplies might arrive by boat along channels connected to the Lemro and Kaladan rivers. In this city, a useful route to market could be wet from end to end.

Water nearby was not always freshwater: tides could make rivers and canals salty. Researchers infer that stored rainfall was therefore a principal supply. Large artificial lakes and smaller tanks scattered among residential areas helped meet the city’s needs. Maintaining those ponds and channels mattered as much as erecting impressive monuments. Their presence alone does not prove that every household had safe water.

The wooden royal palace has disappeared, while parts of its stone enclosure remain on a central rise. Many ordinary buildings were also made of wood, so the city’s surviving stone monuments give an uneven picture of the past. Builders cut substantial stone blocks and sometimes used brick for filling or upper sections. Different materials leave very different archaeological afterlives.

The archaeological area preserves roughly two hundred Buddhist monuments, many from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Carefully fitted stonework, vaulted spaces and carved decoration show the work of skilled builders and artists. These places formed a religious landscape among hills and waterways. The UNESCO page describes a tentative-list submission, rather than an already inscribed World Heritage Site.

Manrique describes an official arriving with attendants carrying drinking water, a betel box and a metal washing vessel. Feet were washed before entering an important person’s house. For this elite visitor, even a social call came with a portable wash kit. The account concerns an official’s entourage, not a complete picture of household bathrooms.

When Manrique became feverish during his stay around 1630, he says the king repeatedly sent a physician. The doctor brought remedies, including a root called lucerrage in the translation. Manrique believed it helped; the editors could not securely identify the plant. This records care offered to a sick visitor, without establishing what illness he had or whether the remedy worked.

sections.title: Poetry, learning and a written voice

items.text: In seventeenth-century Mrauk U, the Bengali poet Alaol describes gatherings hosted by Muslim notables. Dinner, games, dance, music and discussion accompanied poetry at night. Guests could respond to books read aloud. One word, rasa, linked the savor of food with aesthetic pleasure: a good evening could feed both the stomach and the imagination.

Alaol also says he taught reading, song and music to the children of Mrauk U’s nobles. His surviving musical material draws on Sanskrit learned traditions while explaining them in Bengali. This gives a specific glimpse of education in privileged households, where understanding a poem could involve learning how it sounded as well as what it said.

A seventeenth-century Bengali voice survives in fragments attributed to Alaol: “āgama vicāri kahe hīna Alaola”, translated “The humble Alaol speaks after reflecting upon the treatises.” This is d’Hubert’s scholarly Roman transcription, not Bengali script. The musical fragments survive through later textual transmission; no original autograph or exact composition year is claimed.

sections.title: Recovering the city and understanding its ending

items.text: Modern conservation research records more than isolated temples. The Lerici Foundation’s project brought reservoirs, moats, canals, water gates and walls into a geographic information system. Mapping their relationships helps explain how the capital worked as a whole. A pond that looks unremarkable today may be an essential piece of the historical city.

After its seventeenth-century peak, Arakan faced shrinking power and serious struggles at court. Palace guards controlled government from 1692 to 1710, and later rulers had difficulty restoring royal strength. The kingdom nevertheless continued for decades. Its later history cannot be reduced to a single moment when trade stopped or its inhabitants abandoned their culture.

Manrique’s descriptions are vivid, but he wrote to promote a Catholic mission and Portuguese interests. His account was composed after the journeys and published in 1649. Historians compare it with other evidence rather than accepting every dramatic story or population estimate. Reading an eyewitness carefully includes asking what that eyewitness wanted readers to believe.

ending.text: Burmese forces overcame Arakanese resistance in December 1784 and captured Mrauk U in January 1785, ending the independent kingdom. These events changed sovereignty; they did not erase the region’s communities, languages or Buddhist monuments. The atlas’s 1783 seam anticipates the conquest and should not be read as its exact date.
